sources.title: Human History Map 1530 borders
sources.note: Post-contact control demonstrating later New Spain repaint rather than Nahua disappearance.

sources.title: Human History Map researched Mexihcah Triple Alliance card
sources.note: Existing separate card establishes that the Mexica-led alliance already has its own identity and must not absorb all Nahua peoples.

sources.title: INPI National Catalogue: Nahua / Nahuatl people
sources.note: National Indigenous catalogue describes broad geographic distribution, historical dispersal, cultural diversity, and contemporary Nahua communities.

sources.title: Alfredo López Austin, Political organization in Postclassic central Mexico
sources.note: UNAM study stresses that political evidence is regionally uneven and reconstructs multiple central Mexican organizations rather than one Nahua state.

sources.title: William R. Fowler, El complejo Guazapa en El Salvador
sources.note: University of El Salvador archaeological study distinguishes Salvadoran Nawat-speaking Pipil histories, evidence, and debates from central Mexican Nahuatl and Mexica political identity.

sources.title: University of El Salvador, Nahua-Pipil historical framework
sources.note: University research distinguishes Mexican Nahuatl from Central American Nawat and reviews evidence and disagreement about migration chronology.

sources.title: El Salvador Ministry of Culture: Witzapan and the Nawat language
sources.note: Official account documents Nawat as a living language in western El Salvador and describes current intergenerational revitalization.

sources.title: INALI Catalogue of Nahuatl language varieties
sources.note: Official catalog lists distinct Nahuatl varieties, community self-designations, and wide modern geographic references.

sources.title: UNAM Noticonquista: The Triple Alliance among central Mexican Nahuas
sources.note: University history explains the shifting three-part alliance tradition and distinct Nahua political centers.

sources.title: UNAM Noticonquista: The Altepetl
sources.note: University essay defines independent altepetl through water, land, patron deity, ruler, capital, territory, and tributary relationships.

sources.title: UNAM Noticonquista: Tlaxcala, a composite and multiethnic altepetl
sources.note: Study identifies Tlaxcala as independent of Mexica rule, politically complex, and home to Nahuatl speakers and other peoples including Otomi.

sources.title: INAH Guerrero museum: archaeology and pre-Hispanic history
sources.note: Museum synthesis emphasizes three millennia of diverse Guerrero societies, technologies, economies, politics, lifeways, arts, and funerary customs.

sources.title: INAH Ixcateopan archaeological zone
sources.note: Official site history distinguishes Chontal and Nahua actors, Mexica alliances, conquest, and tribute obligations in northern Guerrero.

sources.title: UNAM Noticonquista: Independent territories beyond the Isthmus
sources.note: University account places Ahuizotl-era southern campaigns and trade within contested corridors rather than solid continuous control.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Mexico, 1400 to 1600
sources.note: Museum chronology covers Mexica expansion, the independent Purépecha frontier, and regional political limits.

sources.title: INAH: Templo Mayor
sources.note: Official archaeological record dates Ahuizotl, construction phases, sacred precinct buildings, flood repairs, and continuing excavation.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Tenochtitlan
sources.note: Museum essay covers the lake capital, canals, causeways, neighborhoods, houses, markets, engineering, and urban crafts.

sources.title: INAH: excavated chinampas and canals
sources.note: Archaeological report identifies canal-and-field features in one Tenochtitlan neighborhood and supports a localized chinampa discussion.

sources.title: UNESCO: Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco
sources.note: World Heritage record describes the surviving canal and chinampa landscape while distinguishing it from the whole Nahua world.

sources.title: Digital Florentine Codex, Book 9, folio 1r
sources.note: Postconquest Nahua account of merchant history; useful with explicit 1577 manuscript and retrospective limits.

sources.title: Digital Florentine Codex, Book 8, folio 28v
sources.note: Postconquest Nahua record of palace storage, stewards, foodstuffs, and tribute officers.

sources.title: INAH repository: Mexico, From the Olmecs to the Aztecs
sources.note: Scholarly synthesis discusses foods, clothing, household learning, schools, markets, rank, and the limits of colonial manuscript evidence.

sources.title: University of Kentucky: Codex Mendoza, folio 60 recto
sources.note: University record for the colonial manuscript scenes of age-marked household work and childhood instruction.

sources.title: INAH educational study: Mexica schools
sources.note: Official educational booklet describes calmecac and telpochcalli roles while limiting the evidence to Mexica institutions.

sources.title: Yale eHRAF World Cultures: Aztec culture summary
sources.note: Research summary covers households, rank, gendered work, property, marriage, childhood, and explicit cultural scope.

sources.title: Getty Research Institute: Digital Florentine Codex
sources.note: Project history dates the bilingual alphabetic manuscript to 1577 and names its Nahua authors, artists, and Franciscan frame.

sources.title: INAH Codex Boturini study: pre-Hispanic Nahua pictographic writing
sources.note: Official study explains amoxtli materiality and pictorial, calendrical, logographic, phonetic, numerical, and performative dimensions.

sources.title: UNAM: The first alphabetic records in New Spain
sources.note: Bibliographic study places alphabetic Nahuatl recording after the conquest and distinguishes it from earlier pictorial writing.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Aztec Stone Sculpture
sources.note: Museum essay describes quarrying, carving, grinding, polishing, painting, tools, and the limits of gray surviving surfaces.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: ancient tribute manuscripts
sources.note: Museum essay explains tribute goods and the colonial date and patronage of the Codex Mendoza.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Teponaztli drum
sources.note: Object record describes manufacture, imagery, sound, ceremony, weddings, processions, dances, ballgames, and later use.

sources.title: Digital Florentine Codex, Book 2, folio 3r
sources.note: Postconquest Nahua calendrical account and festival sequence, used with manuscript-date caution.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Tenochtitlan, Templo Mayor
sources.note: Museum essay connects layered construction with Huitzilopochtli, Tlaloc, war, rain, agriculture, and state ceremony.

sources.title: INAH: Huei Tzompantli
sources.note: Official archaeology record documents postholes, skull-built architecture, studied remains, phases, sex and age variation.

sources.title: Digital Florentine Codex, Book 10, folio 108r
sources.note: Postconquest Nahua text records particular plants, washes, drinks, and remedies without proving efficacy or universal practice.

sources.title: Digital Florentine Codex, Book 6, folio 138v
sources.note: Postconquest Nahua account describes midwifery, difficult birth, prayer, embodied intervention, and manuscript editorial context.

sources.title: Tufts University: The Badianus Manuscript
sources.note: University collection dates the illustrated Indigenous medicinal manuscript to 1552 and explains its colonial college setting.

sources.title: UNAM record: potable water and sanitation in Tenochtitlan
sources.note: Scholarly review reports aqueducts, lack of citywide drainage, public and household privies, canoe collection, fertilizer, and dye uses.

sources.title: INAH: Tlaloc and Chapultepec waterworks
sources.note: Official source connects Chapultepec springs, aqueduct engineering, ritual meanings, and Tenochtitlan water supply.

sources.title: INAH: urbanism and architecture at Tlatelolco
sources.note: Archaeological study covers urban water, unequal conduits, drainage, building phases, subsidence, and flood management.

sources.title: INAH Cempoala archaeological guide
sources.note: Official guide dates Cortes arrival in 1519 and describes Totonac Cempoala, Mexica tributary pressure, and the inland alliance route.

sources.title: UNAM Noticonquista: war according to Indigenous conquerors
sources.note: University history treats 1519 to 1521 as a shifting multiethnic Mesoamerican conflict in which autonomous forces pursued local goals.

sources.title: UNAM Noticonquista: military impact of Tenochtitlan fall
sources.note: University account dates the 1521 siege outcome and centers the enormous Indigenous coalition and post-surrender violence.

sources.title: Library of Congress: Huexotzinco Codex, 1531
sources.note: Official object record identifies eight painted amatl panels used by a Nahua community in a colonial taxation lawsuit.
